executive_summary: USD/CHF trades at 0.80944 and EUR/CHF at 0.93758 as of the 2026-08-28 close, with the franc having weakened 0.54% against the dollar and 1.02% against the euro over one month, 3.30% and 3.39% respectively over six months, and 1.32% and 0.35% over one year. The dominant narrative is a policy gap that is still widening: the SNB left its policy rate at 0.00% on 18 June 2026 and conditioned its entire three-year inflation forecast on that rate staying there, while the ECB delivered its first hike since 2023 on 11 June, held at a 2.25% deposit rate on 23 July, and is close to fully priced for a further 25bp on 10 September - taking the EUR-CHF policy spread from 225bp to 250bp inside the tactical window. Valuation does not offset it: the BIS real broad effective exchange rate for Switzerland is 101.69 for June 2026, the 40th percentile of the cached 2024-01 to 2026-06 window and down 1.03 points over one year, so the franc is close to fair rather than stretched, and it now sits at the weak end of its own 52-week ranges against most of the G10 - the 92nd range percentile on EUR/CHF, the 100th on AUD/CHF and the 2nd on CHF/NOK. The central tension is that Switzerland's own fundamentals are the strongest in years - Q2 GDP grew 1.5% quarter-on-quarter on SECO's flash against a 0.2-0.4% consensus, the KOF barometer printed 106.7 in August, its highest since November 2021, industrial production ran +5.5% year-on-year against a -4.7% forecast, and the July trade surplus of CHF 8.1bn was the largest since the series began in 1950 - yet none of it buys a rate rise, because headline CPI is 0.4% and core 0.3%, and the SNB has told the market twice since June that it has an increased willingness to intervene against franc appreciation. We are tactically Bearish CHF at conviction 3 and confidence 62, driven by the rate gap, a risk-on tape with VIX at 14.51 and high-yield spreads at 263bp, and an explicit central bank cap on the currency; we are strategically Neutral at conviction 2 and confidence 54, because a 9.8%-of-GDP current account surplus, a CHF 974bn net international investment position, an AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP and a structurally short speculative market are a floor that the carry deficit cannot break. The caveat is the left tail: with a live Middle East conflict, USD/CHF one-month implied volatility at 6.75% and realised at 8.71%, the market is paying too little for the one scenario that reprices the franc violently.

valuation.trade_weighted_assessment: CAVEAT ON THE VERDICT ABOVE, added on adversarial verification: the 'Fair value' assessment rests on (a) a table that is a relative REER-momentum proxy rather than a purchasing-power-parity level calculation, and (b) a percentile computed on a 30-month window only, from 2024-01 to 2026-06. It should be read as 'not stretched on the available evidence' rather than as a valuation model output. On a trade-weighted basis the franc is unremarkable. The BIS real broad index at 101.69 is 1.7% above its base and 1.03 points lower than a year ago, which places Switzerland in the middle of the G10 real-exchange-rate table between the euro area (102.69, -1.20) and New Zealand (101.12, -3.74), and a long way from Australia (115.92, +10.36) at one end and Japan (65.30, -8.73) at the other. The trade-weighted picture therefore offers neither a valuation reason to buy the franc nor a valuation constraint on selling it.
valuation.what_is_priced_in: Spot is pricing a world in which the SNB stays at zero indefinitely while every peer pays more, and in which the global risk environment stays benign enough that nobody needs a haven. Both of those are correct today and both are already in the price - EUR/CHF at the 92nd percentile of its 52-week range and AUD/CHF at the 100th are not the marks of an under-owned short-franc trade. What is NOT priced is the second leg: the market has taken the June ECB hike and extrapolated a hiking cycle, when the ECB itself has signalled little appetite to go beyond September and Brent has already fallen from 100.31 on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August, removing the impulse that forced the hike in the first place.
valuation.actionability: The valuation signal is structural, not actionable at the tactical horizon: a 40th-percentile REER with a 1.03-point twelve-month decline generates no mean-reversion urgency inside four weeks. It does, however, remove the usual strategic objection to being short the franc, and it is the reason the strategic stance is Neutral rather than Bullish.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since June has been a policy-divergence grind. The Middle East conflict pushed energy prices high enough to force the ECB into its first hike since 2023 on 11 June, while the SNB held at zero and conditioned its whole forecast on staying there, and the franc has been sold steadily against the euro, sterling and the commodity bloc ever since. Price action is orderly rather than violent - EUR/CHF 20-day realised volatility is 4.78% and USD/CHF 8.71% - and the dominant narrative is carry: with CHF the only zero rate in the benchmarking set, the franc is the funding leg of choice in a tape where VIX is 14.51 and high-yield spreads are 263bp. The contradiction sitting underneath is that Swiss activity data has been the best in years, with Q2 GDP at 1.5% quarter-on-quarter, KOF at a four-and-a-half-year high and a record trade surplus, none of which the market is paying for because none of it changes the policy rate. Brent's fall from 100.31 on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August is the first crack in the impulse that started the whole sequence.

tactical.analysis: The SNB policy rate is 0.00% and it is the lowest rate in the G10+SGD benchmarking set by a full 100 basis points, with the Bank of Japan at 1.00% the nearest peer and the Reserve Bank of Australia at 4.35% the furthest. That gap is not merely wide, it is widening inside the tactical window: the ECB delivered its first hike since 2023 on 11 June 2026, taking the deposit rate to 2.25%, held there on 23 July, and a further 25bp to 2.50% at the 10 September Governing Council is close to fully priced, which would take the EUR-CHF policy spread from 225bp to 250bp before this dossier's tactical horizon expires. No other central bank in the set is expected to move in the franc's favour over the same period - the Fed is genuinely two-sided at its 16 September meeting with the target range unchanged at 3.50-3.75% all year, the BoE holds at 3.75% with core CPI stuck at 2.6%, and the Bank of Canada, RBNZ, Norges Bank and Riksbank are all expected to hold. The SNB itself has removed the ambiguity: its June conditional inflation forecast of 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028 is explicitly conditioned on the policy rate being 0% across the entire three-year horizon, which is as close to a rate commitment as an institution that meets four times a year ever gives. The 22 June decision to cut the sight-deposit remuneration threshold factor from 15 to 13.5 with effect from 1 August is plumbing rather than policy - the SNB said explicitly that it 'has no impact on the current monetary policy stance' - but it does push a larger share of sight deposits into the tier that earns the policy rate minus a 0.25pp discount, which firms the money market at the margin and reinforces that the SNB has no intention of using the balance-sheet channel to ease. The term structure says the same thing as the policy rate: the Swiss 10-year at 0.31% yields 416bp less than the US, 452bp less than Australia, 449bp less than the UK and 266bp less than Germany, and the 266bp Bund spread is 41bp wider than the 225bp policy spread, meaning the bond market has already priced ECB tightening beyond the current rate. The one genuine offset is that the franc's carry deficit is entirely known and has been for years, so the marginal information in the next four weeks is not the level of the gap but its direction of change, and the direction of change is against the franc for one more meeting.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices an SNB hold on 24 September with essentially no probability of a move and a small residual tail to -0.25%, and it prices the ECB hike on 10 September at close to certainty. What is not fully priced is the possibility that 10 September is the LAST hike: the ECB has signalled little appetite to tighten beyond September, and Brent falling from 100.31 on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August has already removed much of the impulse that forced the June move. Our read is that the tactical window still belongs to the widening spread, but that the terminal-rate repricing which would stop the franc bleeding is closer than the forward curve implies - perhaps 10-15bp of euro-area terminal rate that is currently priced and should not be.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the carry deficit remains the single largest weight in the framework at 0.24, and it remains against the franc, but the second derivative turns. The euro-area hiking impulse is a response to an energy shock, not to domestic demand: euro-area core HICP was 2.5% in July against headline of 2.9% (corrected from 2.4% on adversarial verification), with the August flash expected near 3.3% on energy, and the ECB has been explicit that it has little appetite to signal further tightening after September. Energy is already reversing, with Brent down 12.07 dollars in a month to 88.24, so the most likely path is that the EUR-CHF policy spread reaches 250bp in September, has a live but non-consensus risk of 275bp by December, and then stops - at which point a 250bp static spread stops generating new franc weakness and simply becomes a level. The Fed is the strategic wildcard in the opposite direction: with the target range unchanged at 3.50-3.75% all year and the September FOMC genuinely two-sided, a US easing cycle beginning in the strategic window would narrow the 362.5bp USD-CHF spread and is the main reason bank consensus targets USD/CHF at 0.78-0.79 by year-end against 0.80944 spot. The Bank of Japan is the quiet second narrowing: core CPI at 1.8% in August supports one more 25bp hike by the 22 January 2027 Outlook Report, which would take the JPY-CHF gap to 125bp and continue the process that has already pushed CHF/JPY down 2.61% over three months. Against that, nothing in the strategic window plausibly moves the SNB - the June forecast is conditioned on 0% for three years, Swiss headline CPI is 0.4% and core 0.3%, and Chairman Schlegel has repeatedly cited the 'undesirable side effects' of negative rates, so the policy rate is pinned at zero with the distribution around it near-symmetric and very tight. The strategic conclusion is therefore Bearish but less so than the tactical: the franc keeps paying away 175bp to 435bp per annum for owning it, and that is a real and permanent drag, but the spread stops widening within the horizon and in the two most important bilaterals - USD and JPY - it more likely narrows.

carry_analysis.carry_regime: Carry is working, and it is working through the classic funding-currency channel rather than through risk appetite alone. With VIX at 14.51 and down 3.70 points over a month, US high-yield spreads at 263bp and 21bp tighter, and investment-grade at 79bp, the environment is exactly the low-volatility grind in which borrowing the zero-rate currency to buy the 4.35% one is rewarded - and AUD/CHF at the 100th percentile of its 52-week close range and CHF/NOK at the 2nd are the receipt. All carry-to-volatility ratios are negative for a long-franc position, which is another way of saying there is no risk-adjusted case for owning the franc on rates alone at any horizon. The regime breaks only if realised volatility rises: USD/CHF 20-day realised is already 8.71% against 6.749% implied, and a move of that magnitude sustained across the crosses would make the carry uneconomic within weeks.
carry_analysis.breakeven_move: Against the euro, a long-franc position pays away 225bp a year, which on EUR/CHF at 0.93758 is 0.0211 per year, 211 pips annualised, or 0.84 pips per trading day. Over a 30-calendar-day tactical horizon (about 21 trading days) EUR/CHF must fall 17.6 pips - from 0.93758 to roughly 0.9358, 0.19% - purely to break even on carry; over the six-month strategic horizon (about 126 trading days) the breakeven is 105 pips, to roughly 0.9271. Against the Australian dollar the arithmetic is harsher: 435bp on AUD/CHF at 0.5797 is 0.0252 a year, 25.2 pips annualised on a pair whose ATR14 is 33 pips, so a long-franc position versus AUD needs AUD/CHF to fall 2.1 pips a month, 12.6 pips over six months, just to stand still - trivial in pips but a permanent 4.35% annual headwind on capital.

tactical.analysis: The Swiss data flow over the last six weeks has been the strongest in years and it has been systematically beating consensus, which is the definition of a tactically supportive surprise regime. SECO's flash estimate put Q2 2026 GDP at +1.5% quarter-on-quarter in real, seasonally adjusted terms against an AWP consensus range of +0.2% to +0.4% - roughly a full percentage point of upside - after +0.4% in Q1 and +0.2% in Q4 2025, with SECO attributing about two-thirds of the growth to industry led by chemicals and pharmaceuticals. The KOF Economic Barometer printed 106.7 in August against a 103.0 forecast and a revised 104.2 prior, its highest level since November 2021 and well above the 100 medium-term average, with KOF citing manufacturing, other services and foreign demand as the drivers. Industrial production for the same period ran +5.5% year-on-year against a -4.7% forecast, a 10.2-point beat, and the ZEW expectations index improved to 12.1 from 10.0 on 26 August. On the price side the picture is the mirror image: headline CPI eased to +0.4% year-on-year in July from +0.5% in June against a +0.5% consensus, month-on-month fell 0.1%, and core inflation - CPI excluding fresh and seasonal products, energy and fuel - held at 0.3%, with services at +0.9% and goods deflation deepening to -0.5% from -0.3% (the headline and core figures are supported by citation [7]; the services and goods split is not carried on that page and is flagged as best available). For a currency, growth that beats without producing inflation is a genuinely mixed signal, but at a two-to-four-week horizon it is net franc-positive through three channels: equity and direct-investment flows into an outperforming economy, the removal of any recession-driven case for SNB easing, and the momentum of the surprise index itself into a dense release calendar. The immediate test is 3 September, when the detailed Q2 GDP print (consensus +1.7% quarter-on-quarter against +0.7% prior) and the August CPI land on the same morning, followed by the 1 September procure.ch PMI at a forecast 54.1 against 53.2. Relative to the peer set the contrast is stark: Swiss GDP of +2.33% year-on-year on the OECD vintage against the euro area's +1.00%, the UK's +1.17% and Canada's +0.99%, with Switzerland's inflation an order of magnitude lower than all of them.

That creates a narrow but real tactical edge into 3 September: consensus for the detailed Q2 print is +1.7% quarter-on-quarter and the risk is skewed higher given the industrial-production beat, while August CPI consensus of 0.0% month-on-month is more likely to undershoot than overshoot with Brent down 12 dollars. A strong-growth, weak-inflation combination is the most franc-ambiguous outcome possible, which is why confidence here is 62 rather than higher.

strategic.analysis: Extending the horizon inverts most of what makes the tactical picture look good, and the reason is tariffs. On 2 April 2026 the United States announced Section 232 tariffs of up to 15% on Swiss pharmaceutical imports, and separate from the HEADLINE tariff regime. On the headline, an earlier framework had cut the rate from 39% to 15%, but adversarial verification against SECO established that this is a November 2025 artefact: following the US Supreme Court striking down the IEEPA reciprocal tariffs on 20 February 2026, the headline regime since 24 July 2026 has been a variable Section 301 tariff of up to 12.5% with MFN credit. The dossier's earlier framing of a live 15% headline rate was corrected on verification and this factor's confidence has been lowered accordingly. Roche and Novartis negotiated three-year shields but every other Swiss drug exporter faces the levy, and pharmaceuticals are close to half of Swiss goods exports to the US. The Q2 GDP surge and the record July trade surplus are therefore very likely to be partly tariff front-running rather than trend demand: chemical and pharmaceutical exports rose 25.7% in July and drove the CHF 8.1bn surplus, the largest since the series began in January 1950, and exports that are pulled forward are exports that will not happen later. The IMF's June Article IV framing of 0.8% growth in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027 and the SNB's own 'around 1%' for 2026 both sit far below the run-rate implied by a +1.5% quarter, which tells you how little of the Q2 print the official sector treats as durable. Switzerland also committed to facilitate at least USD 200bn of investment into the United States over five years, USD 67bn of it in 2026 - a genuine outbound capital flow that partially offsets the current-account surplus and is underdiscussed. On the inflation side the strategic story is stable rather than directional: the SNB forecasts 0.6% for 2026, 0.6% for 2027 and 0.7% for 2028, all comfortably inside the 0-2% band, which means neither a hiking case nor a deflation-driven easing case develops within the horizon. Labour is loosening gently, with registered unemployment up to 3.1% seasonally adjusted from a 2.4% trough earlier in the year, and Swiss wage data is annual with no fresh print inside the freshness window, so the services-inflation persistence question cannot be answered from current data. The honest strategic verdict is Neutral: the growth level is good but the growth impulse is borrowed, the inflation level is stable but too low to matter, and neither side of the mandate generates a directional franc signal over one to six months.

tactical.analysis: The franc is a safe haven and there is currently no demand for a haven. VIX closed at 14.51 on 2026-08-27, down 3.70 points from 18.21 a month earlier and comfortably in the lower quartile of its post-2020 distribution; the CBOE index was 14.43 at the last equity close before the valuation date. US high-yield spreads at 263bp have tightened 21bp over the month and investment-grade sits at 79bp, both near the tight end of the post-2022 range, while the S&P 500 finished at 7,711.76 and the Nasdaq at 26,402.42 close to their highs. This is the textbook low-volatility risk-on tape in which the franc's structural bid is absent and its funding-currency role dominates - and the cross-section confirms it, with AUD/CHF at the 100th percentile of its 52-week close range, NZD/CHF at the 95th, SGD/CHF at the 97th and CHF/NOK at the 0th. What makes the configuration remarkable, and worth flagging rather than glossing, is that this is happening with an active Middle East conflict that forced the ECB into its first hike since 2023 on 11 June and then pushed Brent to 100.31 on 24 July - the energy peak followed the hike by six weeks rather than preceding it, a sequencing point corrected on adversarial verification. Markets have de-risked the geopolitics: Brent has already fallen back to 88.24 as of 2026-08-25 and VIX has fallen with it. The one dissenting signal is gold, which at 4,456.44 on 2026-08-28 is up 8.60% over a month and 22.39% over a year - the franc's traditional correlate is being bought hard while the franc itself is being sold, which is a correlation breakdown rather than confirmation. The most likely explanation is that gold is absorbing the sovereign-debasement and reserve-diversification bid while the franc, which pays 0% and is explicitly capped by its own central bank, is a poor vehicle for the same trade. For the next two to four weeks the risk factor is therefore clearly franc-negative, and the honest caveat is that this is the factor most capable of reversing without warning.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market is priced for the Middle East conflict to stay contained, and the evidence for that pricing is Brent 12 dollars off its July high with VIX at 14.51 and high-yield at 263bp. That is a coherent view but it is a one-sided one, and the franc is the cheapest way to be on the other side of it. The specific mispricing is the divergence between gold, up 8.60% in a month on haven and debasement demand, and the franc, down against seven of nine crosses over the same period - historically these move together, and the gap is a signal that franc haven demand is being under-bid rather than that haven demand has disappeared.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the risk factor stops being a directional read and becomes an options position, and at VIX 14.51 with high-yield at 263bp the distribution is not symmetric. Credit and equity volatility are close to the tight end of their post-2022 ranges, which mechanically limits how much further they can compress and leaves considerably more room to widen than to tighten - and the franc's payoff is convex in exactly that direction. The live catalysts are identifiable rather than hypothetical: the Middle East conflict that produced a 30-dollar Brent round trip between June and August is unresolved, the SNB itself named 'the uncertain geopolitical situation' and the risk of strong franc appreciation as its principal concern in the June assessment, and a euro-area economy being tightened into an energy shock is a plausible source of European credit stress to which the franc is the closest and most liquid hedge. Against that, three things argue the franc will not capture the full haven bid even if one arrives. First, gold has demonstrably taken share, rising 8.60% in a month while the franc fell. Second, the yen is competing directly and winning - CHF/JPY is down 2.61% over three months with the BoJ normalising and Japanese core CPI at 1.8%. Third, and most importantly, the SNB has explicitly told the market it has an increased willingness to intervene against rapid franc appreciation, which truncates the right tail of any haven rally. The net of a fat, unpriced left tail against a policy-truncated right tail is genuinely Neutral: the risk factor will not drive the franc lower over six months from here because it is already at an extreme, but nor can it be relied upon to drive it higher.

tactical.analysis: Positioning has just finished doing the thing that would have made it a signal, and is now a non-signal. The aggregate CFTC speculative net position in Swiss franc futures was -19.9k contracts at the 2026-08-28 release (data as of Tuesday 25 August), having covered from -32.5k released 14 August (as of 11 August) and -27.3k released 21 August (as of 18 August). Sourcing note: citation [31] carries the 21 August article containing only the -27.3k and -32.5k readings; the -19.9k figure comes from the pipeline event calendar and is flagged as not directly supported by that link - roughly 40% of the aggregate short bought back in three weeks, the fastest covering run of the year. Against the roughly -40k to 0 band the franc has occupied over the past twelve months that places current positioning close to the midpoint, at an estimated 48th percentile, which is precisely the level at which positioning generates no contrarian information. The cached tranche as of 2026-08-11 - which is the same observation date as the -32.5k released on 14 August, two weeks rather than three behind the headline, corrected on verification - shows the internal structure: total open interest 109,874 contracts, leveraged funds net -11,432 (only 10.4% of open interest, and extended by 1,348 contracts that week), asset managers net -38,322, and dealers the long counterparty at +62,382. That split is the classic funding-currency configuration - real money is the persistent structural seller of the franc while fast money trades around it - and it means the headline short is less fragile than a leveraged-fund-driven short of the same size would be. The currency brief's own threshold is that net specs beyond plus or minus 30,000 contracts are notable for the franc given its smaller open interest than EUR or JPY; at -19.9k the market is inside that band, so there is capacity for shorts to be rebuilt into the 10 September ECB hike without hitting an extreme. On the official-flow side, SNB foreign currency reserves rose from CHF 759bn in June to CHF 768bn in July and total official reserve assets from CHF 879.9bn to CHF 889.6bn at the 2026-08-31 release, but with the franc weakening and gold up 8.60% over the month that build is far more consistent with valuation and investment income than with active franc selling. The weekly sight-deposit series - the sharper intervention proxy - could not be refreshed from a free source this cycle and the last available reading is CHF 469.27bn total for the week ending 2026-07-24, which is stale and flagged as such.

What is priced now is a neutral book going into a franc-negative catalyst, which historically is the configuration that allows a trend to extend rather than reverse. strategic.analysis: Over one to six months positioning stops being about the headline net and starts being about who holds it and how quickly they can move. The asset-manager short of -38,322 contracts is the strategically important number - with the caveat, added on adversarial verification, that it is observed as of 11 August and the aggregate has covered 12,600 contracts since, so the real-money leg has very probably reduced too and -38,322 should be read as an upper bound rather than a current level: it is more than three times the leveraged-fund position, it represents roughly USD 5.92bn of notional against a total open interest of only 109,874 contracts, and real-money shorts are slow to build and slower to unwind, which means they behave like a coiled spring rather than like a stop-loss. The franc's structural condition is to be sold - it is the funding currency of choice at 0.00% against a set in which the median peer pays 2.5% - and that structural short is the raw material of every violent franc squeeze in the historical record, including the January 2015 floor removal that moved EUR/CHF roughly 30% intraday. Over a six-month window containing an unresolved Middle East conflict, a euro-area central bank tightening into an energy shock, and a Fed whose next move is genuinely two-sided, the probability of at least one event capable of forcing that position to cover is materially above zero. The asymmetry is what makes this Bullish rather than Neutral: from -19.9k aggregate there is perhaps 20,000 contracts of room to extend shorts before hitting the brief's plus or minus 30,000 'notable' threshold, but there is 58,000 contracts of asset-manager and leveraged-fund exposure that would have to be bought back in a squeeze. tactical.analysis: Switzerland's external accounts are producing record numbers and they are doing it right now, which makes this factor tactically relevant despite its low 0.06 tactical weight. The July 2026 trade surplus widened to CHF 8.1bn from CHF 3.8bn in June - the largest since the series began in January 1950 - on exports up 13.8% in nominal terms to CHF 27.79bn and imports down 4.5% to CHF 19.65bn, with chemical and pharmaceutical products up 25.7%, watch exports rising for a second consecutive month at +5.8%, and shipments to Europe up 22.9%. The pipeline calendar records the same release at 8.73 against a 5.049 prior. Adversarial verification could not corroborate 8.73 from any independent source - the corroborated range is CHF 8.1bn to 8.4bn - so the calendar value is flagged as unverified and possibly a transposition, and the nominal CHF 8.1bn figure from the customs office is the one relied upon here. On the flow side the current account ran CHF 16bn in Q1 2026, which the OECD vintage places at 9.77% of GDP - the second highest in the benchmarking set behind Norway's 15.59% and more than five times the euro area's 1.93% - while the net international investment position rose CHF 18bn quarter-on-quarter to CHF 974bn. A surplus of that scale is a continuous, mechanical, price-insensitive bid for francs that operates every day regardless of the policy rate, and it is the reason the franc has appreciated in real terms over decades despite paying nothing. The franc-relevant commodity channel is gold rather than trade: Switzerland is the world's largest refining hub, XAU/USD is at 4,456.44 and up 8.60% over a month, and the shared safe-haven correlation is mildly franc-supportive. As a net energy importer Switzerland also gains directly from Brent's fall from 100.31 to 88.24, which is a terms-of-trade improvement worth more to Switzerland than to the euro area on a per-unit-of-GDP basis. The offsets are real but slower-moving: the Q1 current account was CHF 11bn lower than a year earlier, driven by goods trade and a swing in the non-monetary gold balance from surplus to deficit, and the services balance remained negative at -CHF 2.9bn.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market treats the Swiss external surplus as wallpaper - a permanent feature that never surprises and therefore never trades. That is mostly correct and it is why this factor carries only 0.06 tactical weight, but a record 76-year high in the trade surplus arriving in the same month as a one-percentage-point GDP beat is not wallpaper, and it is not in the price at all. The 17 September trade release against an 8.73 prior is the tactical test; a second consecutive record would begin to force the flow story into the narrative.

strategic.analysis: At the strategic horizon this factor carries the heaviest weight after policy at 0.16, and it is where the bull case for the franc actually lives. A current account of 9.77% of GDP is not a cyclical number; it is the product of a goods surplus in pharmaceuticals, precision engineering and watches, a services surplus in financial and commodity-trading revenue, and a large primary income surplus thrown off by a net international investment position of CHF 974bn - roughly 120% of annual GDP. That structure generates a persistent excess of franc receipts over franc payments which must either be repatriated, hedged or absorbed by the official sector, and it is the fundamental reason the Swiss real effective exchange rate has trended higher for decades and the reason the SNB has accumulated CHF 889.6bn of official reserve assets leaning against it. Nothing in the strategic window changes that structure. What does change at the margin, and what keeps confidence at 80 rather than higher, is the tariff and investment offset. US Section 232 pharmaceutical tariffs of up to 15% announced on 2 April 2026 apply to every Swiss drug exporter except Roche and Novartis, and pharmaceuticals are close to half of Swiss goods exports to the United States - the July surge of 25.7% almost certainly contains front-running that will reverse inside the horizon. Switzerland has also committed to facilitate at least USD 200bn of investment into the US over five years, USD 67bn of it in 2026, which is an outbound capital flow equal to a meaningful fraction of the annual current-account surplus and is the most underdiscussed franc-negative item in the whole picture. Even netting those, the arithmetic does not reverse: a 9.77%-of-GDP surplus against a euro area at 1.93%, a UK at -2.84% and a US at -2.85% is a structural differential that dominates any six-month cyclical swing, and it is what stops the strategic stance being Bearish despite a 225 to 435 basis point carry deficit.

tactical.analysis: The SNB gives almost no forward guidance in the conventional sense - three people meeting four times a year, no dot plot, no rate path - but in June 2026 it gave the market something more useful and more directional: an explicit, one-sided statement of its reaction function to the exchange rate. The 18 June assessment reads 'If necessary, the SNB has an increased willingness to intervene in the foreign exchange market. The SNB thereby counters a rapid and excessive appreciation of the Swiss franc, which would jeopardise price stability in Switzerland.' That is not symmetric language. There is no corresponding commitment to lean against franc weakness, and there is no plausible level of franc depreciation at which a central bank forecasting 0.6% inflation would object. Chairman Schlegel then reaffirmed the same formulation on 8 July in Zurich, coupling it with 'medium-term inflationary pressure virtually unchanged', and has separately stated that the SNB has 'unrestricted room for manoeuvre' on both the policy rate and intervention. For a currency trader that is a written option: the central bank has told you it will sell the franc if it rallies hard and will do nothing if it falls. The credibility to enforce it is not in question - the SNB holds CHF 889.6bn of official reserve assets, more than 100% of GDP, and its historical record of acting on FX is the strongest in the developed world. The one genuine credibility scar is January 2015, when the EUR/CHF floor was removed without warning and the pair moved roughly 30% intraday; that episode is why nobody assumes SNB guidance binds indefinitely, and it is the reason confidence here is 72 rather than 85. The single tactical event is the 24 September assessment, where a new conditional inflation forecast will be published and where the operative question is not the rate - a hold at 0.00% is effectively certain - but whether the intervention sentence survives intact.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months guidance carries almost double the weight it does tactically, at 0.12, and it is the most durable of the franc-negative factors because it is a statement about the reaction function rather than about the data. The SNB's mandate is price stability with 'due account of economic developments', and in practice that has always meant a central bank acutely sensitive to franc strength because Switzerland's economy is export-dependent - roughly half of goods exports to the United States are pharmaceutical, and those exports are now facing a 15% Section 232 tariff, which raises rather than lowers the SNB's sensitivity to any additional loss of competitiveness through the exchange rate. Whatever the SNB says on 24 September, its structural incentive over the next six months is to prefer a softer franc, and its stated tool preference is intervention rather than negative rates: Schlegel has repeatedly cited the 'undesirable side effects' of sub-zero policy, Switzerland ran negative rates from December 2014 to September 2022 and the institutional memory is poor, and the sell-side consensus has converged on intervention as the active lever with the rate held at 0.00% through 2026. The credibility of that framework is high and the balance sheet behind it is effectively unlimited relative to Swiss GDP. The strategic risk to this view is not that the SNB reverses - it is that the SNB becomes irrelevant, which happens if the franc weakens far enough that intervention is unnecessary and the guidance simply stops binding; at that point the factor goes quiet rather than turning franc-positive. There is also a genuine tail in the other direction: a central bank that surprised the market by 30% in January 2015 is capable of surprising it again, and if Swiss inflation were to fall back towards zero on the back of Brent at 88.24 and a firm franc, the possibility of a return to negative rates - currently a small tail, perhaps 10 to 15% by mid-2027 - would reappear and would be sharply franc-negative.

tactical.analysis: Event risk is the one factor where the franc's asymmetry runs in its own favour, and the next four weeks are unusually dense. The dated Swiss-specific item is the federal referendum on 27 September 2026 on writing neutrality into the constitution in a form that would bar Switzerland from joining sanctions against belligerent states absent a UN Security Council mandate and would constrain military cooperation with NATO. Tamedia/20 Minuten polling from roughly 19-21 August has 62% against and 36% in favour, so rejection is the strong base case and the modal outcome is a non-event. Note on sourcing: citation [16] carries an EARLIER Leewas/Tamedia poll of 11-14 June at 54% opposed and 34% in favour; the 62/36 figures come from the later August poll and could not be tied to a free primary link, so they are best available and flagged. The tail matters more than the mode, because passage would force a re-examination of Switzerland's alignment with the EU and US sanctions architecture - CHF 8.5bn of financial assets plus property, vehicles, aircraft and art were frozen in Switzerland under the Russia regime as of 1 July 2026 - and would cut both ways for the haven premium, arguably enhancing the neutrality claim while raising secondary-sanctions and market-access friction. The larger and undated risk is the Middle East, which forced the ECB into its first hike since 2023 on 11 June and then drove Brent from 100.31 on 24 July down 12.0% to 88.24 on 25 August; the SNB explicitly named 'the uncertain geopolitical situation' and the risk of strong franc appreciation as its principal concern. On the other side, the Swiss-specific event risk that is unambiguously franc-negative is trade: the Section 232 pharmaceutical tariff regime of up to 15%, announced on 2 April 2026 and effective 31 July 2026, is live and its enforcement details are still evolving. Note that the separate HEADLINE tariff is no longer the 15% framework rate: verification against SECO established a variable Section 301 rate of up to 12.5% with MFN credit since 24 July 2026. Netting these, the tactical event distribution is skewed franc-positive - the plausible shocks that move the franc 2% or more in four weeks are overwhelmingly risk-off shocks - but the probability-weighted expectation is small, which is why the stance is Bullish at only 55.

strategic.analysis: Over one to six months the event set broadens and the skew persists. The Middle East conflict is the organising fact of the 2026 macro regime: it produced the energy shock that forced the ECB to hike in June, it is the reason global inflation forecasts were revised up, and it remains unresolved with Brent having fallen 12.0% from 100.31 on 24 July to 88.24 on 25 August. Of 318 consultation submissions a clear majority of political, economic and cantonal stakeholders were supportive, so this is a slow, probably successful process - but a referendum defeat at any point over the next two years would be a genuine Swiss-specific negative through the market-access channel, and it sits just outside the strategic window rather than safely beyond it. Third, the concentration of the Swiss banking system in a single institution following the 2023 absorption of Credit Suisse means any UBS-specific stress is systemic for the franc; no fresh 2026 development was identified this cycle, so this is a monitored but undated risk. Fourth, the pharmaceutical tariff regime remains the principal Swiss-specific economic threat and is franc-negative. tactical.analysis: Swiss fiscal and sovereign risk is, as the currency brief anticipates, not currently material, and the correct tactical stance is Neutral held with high confidence in the assessment rather than low confidence in the currency. Switzerland is rated AAA by every major agency; Morningstar DBRS reconfirmed AAA with a Stable trend on 16 January 2026, and Switzerland is one of roughly eleven remaining AAA sovereigns globally. General government debt stood at 37.6% of GDP in 2024 on the rating-agency measure, among the lowest in the developed world and less than half the ratio of every other G10 sovereign bar Norway. The measure matters and was flagged on adversarial verification: the IMF puts Swiss general-government gross debt at 40.7% of GDP for 2025, while the Maastricht-basis figure runs nearer 30%. The range of 30% to 41% across definitions does not change the conclusion, but 37.6% should be read as one measure among three rather than as a single hard number, and the 2003 debt brake mandates budget balance over the business cycle with higher expenditure requiring higher revenue or offsetting cuts. The fiscal balance was an estimated surplus of 0.4% of GDP in 2025 with the IMF projecting surpluses averaging around 0.2% out to 2028. There is no bond supply story: the Confederation issues very little, auctions are not a market event, and the Swiss 10-year at 0.31% on the monthly series to 2026-06-01 remains by far the lowest in the benchmarking set - 266bp below Germany and 416bp below the United States. Swiss sovereign CDS is not quoted on any accessible source and is functionally meaningless at these credit metrics, which is itself the finding. The reason this is Neutral rather than Bullish tactically is that none of it changes inside four weeks and none of it is a source of surprise: there is no scheduled Swiss budget event, no rating review, and no auction of consequence in the tactical window, so the factor generates a level of quality without generating a directional impulse. The one thing worth watching is the opposite tail - a fiscal deterioration among peers rather than in Switzerland - which would be franc-positive through the relative-quality channel.

Switzerland's 37.6% debt-to-GDP on the rating-agency measure - 40.7% on the IMF's, nearer 30% on the Maastricht basis, all flagged - with a structural surplus and a constitutional debt brake is not merely good; it is an outlier in a developed world where fiscal trajectories are broadly deteriorating - the United States runs a current-account deficit of 2.85% of GDP alongside a large and rising primary deficit, the UK carries a 2.84% external deficit with a heavy gilt supply calendar, and euro-area sovereign debt dynamics are being tested by an ECB that is now tightening rather than easing. In a six-month window in which policy rates are rising in the euro area and the US term premium is expanding, with DGS30 at 5.19% and DGS10 at 4.67% on 2026-08-27 and the US 2s10s having steepened to +39bp, the relative attractiveness of a AAA sovereign with a 0.31% ten-year and no supply problem increases rather than decreases. This is the mechanism by which fiscal quality becomes an FX factor: it is not that Switzerland gets better, it is that the alternatives get worse, and reserve managers and long-term allocators respond to relative rather than absolute quality. The AAA rating is also what underwrites the SNB's own capacity to hold CHF 889.6bn of official reserve assets without any market question about the sovereign standing behind them, which is a second-order but real support. Confidence is 66 rather than higher because the transmission from fiscal quality to spot is slow, diffuse and hard to date, and because the franc's 0.31% yield means the quality bid must be expressed through the currency rather than through the bond, which is a weaker channel.

weighted_score.interpretation: A net score of -0.0499 is effectively flat and sits comfortably inside the neutral band of -0.10 to +0.10. The structure behind it is far more interesting than the number: this is not a score built from ten indifferent factors but from two large opposing blocs that nearly cancel. On the bearish side, Policy & Rates contributes -0.1824 and Guidance & Credibility -0.0900, a combined -0.2724 representing the carry deficit and the SNB's explicit asymmetric cap on the currency. On the bullish side, External Balance contributes +0.1216 at its heavy 0.16 strategic weight, Fiscal & Sovereign +0.0434, Event Risk +0.0275 and Flows +0.0300, a combined +0.2225 representing a near-10%-of-GDP current account, a AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP, an unresolved geopolitical tail and a concentrated real-money short. Three factors score zero - Inflation & Growth, Risk Appetite and USD Liquidity - and in each case the zero is a genuine two-sided assessment rather than an absence of analysis.
weighted_score.mapping_to_conviction: A net score between -0.10 and +0.10 maps to a Neutral stance at conviction 2 of 5, where conviction 1 would indicate no usable information and conviction 3 would require a net score beyond 0.10 in either direction. Conviction 2 rather than 1 is justified because the neutrality here is a genuine balance of two large, well-identified and opposing forces - each worth roughly 0.25 of weighted score - rather than an absence of signal, which makes the composition of the neutrality actionable even though its direction is not.

strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the dossier becomes a contest between two structural facts, and they very nearly cancel. On one side, Policy & Rates retains its 0.24 weight and Guidance & Credibility nearly doubles to 0.12, so a franc that pays 0.00% against a set whose median peer pays 2.50%, and whose central bank has told the market twice since June that it has an increased willingness to intervene against appreciation, contributes a combined -0.2724. On the other, External Balance rises to 0.16 and Fiscal & Sovereign to 0.07, so a current account of 9.77% of GDP, a net international investment position of CHF 974bn worth roughly 120% of annual output, a AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP with a constitutional debt brake, an unresolved Middle East conflict and a -38,322 contract asset-manager short contribute a combined +0.2225. The net of -0.0499 is as close to flat as this framework produces, and the honest conclusion is that the franc's carry deficit is real and permanent but is very nearly fully offset by the balance-of-payments and quality bid underneath it. The factors interact rather than merely summing: the same central bank asymmetry that makes Guidance bearish is what makes Flows bullish, because a policy-capped currency with a structural surplus attracts a persistent real-money short that becomes squeeze fuel; and the same external surplus that makes Factor 5 bullish is what forces the SNB to lean against the franc in the first place. What is priced is captured in bank consensus - USD/CHF at 0.78 to 0.79 by year-end from J.P. Morgan, MUFG and UBS, and EUR/CHF at 0.94 to 0.96 from UBS, SEB, Scotiabank, Citi and ING - which is a market that is simultaneously long the franc against the dollar and short it against the euro, coherent only if the dollar falls further than the franc does. Our expectation of USD/CHF 0.7950 and EUR/CHF 0.9450 at six months sits inside that consensus but is deliberately less aggressive on both legs, because we think the ECB hiking cycle ends sooner than the terminal-rate pricing implies and the September FOMC genuinely contains a hike. The path of least resistance is range-bound: EUR/CHF between roughly 0.9200 and 0.9600, USD/CHF between 0.7800 and 0.8300, with the franc weak enough that carry is earned and strong enough that the surplus is absorbed. Key dated catalysts are the ECB on 10 September, 29 October and 17 December, the FOMC on 16 September, 28 October and 9 December, the SNB assessments on 24 September and 10 December, and the neutrality referendum on 27 September. The conviction driver is not direction but composition: knowing that the neutrality is the sum of a -0.28 carry-and-guidance bloc and a +0.23 structural bloc tells you exactly which data would break the tie, and the answer is any sustained rise in realised volatility. Actionability is therefore in relative value and convexity rather than in outright direction, and that is a genuine conclusion rather than a hedge.

consensus_divergence.our_view: We are tactically Bearish the franc at conviction 3 and strategically Neutral at conviction 2, with a six-month expectation of USD/CHF 0.7950 and EUR/CHF 0.9450. That is inside the consensus band on both legs but deliberately less aggressive on each: less franc-bullish than consensus against the dollar, and less franc-bearish than consensus against the euro. In other words we think the market is right about the direction of both legs and is over-extrapolating the magnitude of both.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Roughly 100-150 pips versus consensus on USD/CHF (our 0.7950 against a 0.78-0.79 cluster) and roughly 50-150 pips on EUR/CHF (our 0.9450 against a 0.95-0.96 cluster). The divergence is modest in level but material in shape: consensus implies a trade-weighted franc that is essentially unchanged achieved through two large offsetting moves, whereas we expect two smaller ones.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: Three factors are being underweighted by consensus. First, the terminal ECB rate: the market has taken the June hike and the near-certain September hike and extrapolated a cycle, when the ECB has signalled little appetite to go further and Brent has already fallen 12.07 dollars from its July high, removing the energy impulse that forced the move - which caps how far EUR/CHF can run. Second, the September FOMC is genuinely two-sided with headline PCE near 4% and core above 3%, so a consensus predicated on Fed easing driving USD/CHF to 0.78 is carrying a directional bet that is not yet in the data. Third, and most importantly, consensus is pricing a modal path with no allowance for the distribution around it: a 9.77%-of-GDP current account, a -38,322 contract asset-manager short and an unresolved Middle East conflict together mean the franc's left tail is much fatter than a 7.112% six-month implied volatility implies, and every consensus forecast in the set is implicitly short that tail.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: Being right delivers a modest 100-150 pip advantage on each leg versus consensus, but the real payoff is structural: it means the correct expression is size-limited spot for the tactical view plus separately owned long-dated franc convexity, rather than the leveraged directional carry position that consensus targets imply.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If consensus is right and the ECB tightens through December while the Fed eases, EUR/CHF reaches 0.96 and USD/CHF 0.78 simultaneously - our EUR/CHF call is wrong by 150 pips and our USD/CHF call by 150 pips in opposite directions, so a trade-weighted franc expression loses on both legs. cross_horizon_consistency.summary: The horizons are not aligned: tactically Bearish at conviction 3 with a net score of -0.2358, strategically Neutral at conviction 2 with a net score of -0.0499. The divergence is genuine and mechanistic rather than a hedge - four of the ten factors change stance between horizons, and each change has an identifiable cause.
cross_horizon_consistency.divergence_explanation: The tactical bearish case is a bet on a scheduled event and a prevailing regime: the ECB takes the euro-franc spread from 225bp to 250bp on 10 September while VIX at 14.51 and abundant dollar funding keep the carry trade alive. Both of those are time-limited. The strategic neutrality is the recognition that once the ECB stops - which it has signalled it intends to do after September - a static 250bp spread stops generating new franc weakness and simply becomes a cost, at which point the structural bloc reasserts: a 9.77%-of-GDP current account, a CHF 974bn net international investment position, a AAA sovereign at 37.6% debt-to-GDP and a -38,322 contract real-money short that is squeeze fuel. Factor 2 flips from Bullish to Neutral because Q2's growth surge is pharmaceutical front-running ahead of the 15% Section 232 tariff and unwinds inside the strategic window; Factor 3 flips from Bearish to Neutral because a compressed volatility regime is a reliable four-week signal and an unreliable six-month one; Factor 4 flips from Neutral to Bullish as the question changes from 'is positioning stretched' to 'what happens if it has to cover'; and Factor 10 flips from Bearish to Neutral as the softening dollar catches up with the easy funding.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: Late October to mid-November 2026. The specific marker is the 29 October ECB Governing Council: if the ECB holds at 2.50% there, the widening phase of the euro-franc spread is complete and the tactical thesis has run its course. A secondary marker is the Q4 2026 Swiss data, where the pharmaceutical front-running that produced a +1.5% Q2 should begin to reverse.
cross_horizon_consistency.catalyst_for_transition: The ECB explicitly signalling the end of its tightening cycle - most likely at the 29 October or 17 December meeting - combined with the 31 December year-end dollar funding squeeze and, potentially, the first Fed cut. Any sustained rise in USD/CHF realised volatility above 10% would accelerate the transition by making the CHF-funded carry trade uneconomic.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Run the tactical short-franc view in size-limited spot with a defined horizon that expires around the 29 October ECB rather than being rolled indefinitely, and hold the strategic view as long franc convexity rather than as spot. The two are complementary rather than contradictory: the spot leg earns 225bp of carry on EUR/CHF while the option leg is being sold to you at an estimated 30th-percentile implied volatility with no event premium in the term structure.

seasonality.pattern: Two documented seasonal patterns are relevant to the franc inside these horizons. The first is the 31 December dollar-funding turn: year-end balance-sheet compression at dealer banks reliably widens cross-currency basis, which raises the cost of funding non-dollar assets in dollars and forces a reduction of carry positions - a mechanically franc-supportive flow, because the franc is the funding leg being bought back. The second is generic year-end portfolio rebalancing, in which unhedged foreign-asset gains accumulated through the year are partially repatriated by Swiss institutional investors. Neither pattern is Swiss-specific in origin, and there is no documented Swiss fiscal-year or earnings-season hedging cycle equivalent to Japan's March-September repatriation or Australia's August earnings hedging.
seasonality.relevance_window: Outside the 2-4 week tactical horizon entirely. Inside the 1-6 month strategic horizon: the year-end turn typically begins to be priced into forwards from early November and peaks in the final two weeks of December, so it falls in the back third of the strategic window.
seasonality.historical_magnitude: Year-end basis widening in the three-month EUR/USD pair has historically ranged from a few basis points in calm years to 30-40bp in stressed ones. With the basis last observed at only -16 to -20bp in mid-May 2026 (stale, flagged), materially tighter than the -35 to -45bp regime of 2023, there is more room than usual for a widening. The FX impact is typically worth well under 1% on the franc crosses and is a supporting consideration rather than a thesis.
seasonality.current_alignment: Aligned with the strategic view rather than the tactical one. The seasonal effect is franc-supportive and arrives in the phase-two window identified in the path expectation, reinforcing the expectation that the franc's weakest period is September to October and that it firms into the new year.

assumptions: Convention: this dossier is written from the franc's perspective, but USD/CHF and EUR/CHF are quoted as francs per unit of counter currency. 'Bullish CHF' therefore means USD/CHF and EUR/CHF FALLING. CHF/JPY, CHF/NOK and CHF/SEK are quoted the conventional way, so a rising rate on those three means a stronger franc. Every directional statement in this dossier has been written to state the franc direction explicitly.

All spot rates, moving averages, ATR, realised volatility, 52-week ranges, range percentiles and support/resistance zones are taken from the pipeline's gated price store as of the 2026-08-28 close and are not recomputed. Realised volatility is read directly from the derived per-pair files (20-day and 60-day, annualised on 252 weekday observations) rather than estimated, in line with the framework's requirement that the carry-to-volatility denominator not be re-derived.

Sovereign 10-year yields, including the Swiss 0.31%, are MONTHLY series with an as-of date of 2026-06-01. They are used for bilateral spread analysis and are flagged as monthly at every point of use; they must not be read as live levels. Note explicitly: at 92 days old they breach BOTH the 30-day tactical and 60-day strategic freshness windows, and no free source could refresh them this cycle. The Swiss 2-year yield could not be sourced from any free provider this cycle, so the Swiss 2s10s curve shape is a documented gap and the US curve is quoted instead for reference.

Central bank meeting dates are taken from the pipeline's authoritative meetings calendar and were not web-searched. Where a secondary source quotes a different SNB date (for example 25 September, which is the 2025 cycle date), the calendar value of 2026-09-24 governs. SGD is absent from the meetings calendar by design because MAS operates an S$NEER band rather than a policy rate.

The implied-volatility percentile of 30 is an estimate derived from the relationship between current implied and realised volatility rather than a computed one-year percentile.

25-delta risk reversals for USD/CHF and EUR/CHF could not be sourced from any free provider this cycle and are recorded as a documented gap rather than estimated. The direct three-month CHF/USD cross-currency basis is likewise unquoted; the approximately -45bp figure used is DERIVED as the cached USD/CHF futures-implied roll premium of -407.7bp annualised less the 362.5bp policy differential, and is labelled a derivation at every point of use.

Forward points and outright forwards for USD/CHF are derived from the same -4.077% annualised futures roll premium applied linearly across the 1-month, 3-month and 6-month tenors. They are not quoted outright forwards and will differ from a dealer quote by the term structure of the basis.

The PPP deviation table is NOT a purchasing-power-parity level calculation. No free OECD PPP extract was available this cycle, so the table is constructed as a REER-momentum proxy: the deviation is the Swiss BIS real broad effective exchange rate one-year change of -1.03 minus each peer's one-year change, and the implied fair value reverses that relative real move at current spot. It measures relative real-exchange-rate momentum over twelve months, not an absolute valuation level, and should be read accordingly.

The BIS REER historical percentile of 40 is computed against the cached 2024-01 to 2026-06 window only, consistent with the methodology used in the prior cycle's CHF dossier, and is not a long-history percentile.

The macro comparison table mixes measurement bases where necessary and each instance is labelled in the row. Swiss GDP is the OECD vintage (+1.87% quarter-on-quarter) for cross-currency comparability rather than SECO's official +1.5% flash; Swiss unemployment is the ILO-harmonised quarterly rate of 5.07% for 2026-Q1 (OECD vintage 2026-06-16 - note this is high against Switzerland's usual ILO range of roughly 4.3-4.8% and is flagged) rather than SECO's registered 3.1% seasonally adjusted for July 2026, because the peer rows are also harmonised measures. Core CPI is carried as a genuine core measure only for CHF, EUR, GBP, JPY and (approximately) USD; for CAD, AUD, NZD, NOK and SEK the headline is carried as an explicitly labelled proxy because the preferred core measures are not in the pipeline cache and were not separately sourced. Every SGD macro cell is null because Singapore is not an OECD member and has no cached vintages.

Japan's headline CPI was not separately sourced this cycle; the 1.8% core figure for August 2026 is carried in both the headline and core columns of the macro table and is flagged in the row. The US core figure of 3.10% is an approximation of the reported 'core above 3%' and is flagged as an estimate rather than a cached print.

The market-implied SNB policy path is INFERRED rather than quoted: no free SARON OIS strip was available. The inference of a flat 0.00% over six months with a sub-15% tail to -0.25% rests on the SNB's own forecast being conditioned on 0% through 2028, on sell-side consensus for a hold through 2026, and on Chairman Schlegel's repeated dismissal of negative rates.

SNB weekly sight deposits, the sharpest intervention proxy, could not be refreshed for August 2026 from a free source. The reading of CHF 469.27bn total and CHF 442.66bn domestic banks for the week ending 2026-07-24 is carried forward from the prior cycle and is explicitly flagged as stale; the monthly foreign-reserve series (CHF 759bn to CHF 768bn, June to July 2026) is used as the substitute.

Swiss wage growth is an annual FSO series with no print inside the 60-day strategic freshness window, and no Citi Economic Surprise Index for Switzerland is available on a free source. In place of the latter, a five-release surprise tally has been constructed from the pipeline event calendar and is described as such.

The Swiss trade balance is reported on two bases that differ: CHF 8.1bn nominal from the Federal Office for Customs and Border Security versus 8.73 on the pipeline calendar's series (prior 5.049 versus 3.8). Adversarial verification could NOT corroborate 8.73 from any independent source - the corroborated range is 8.1bn to 8.37bn - so the calendar figure is flagged as unverified and possibly a transposition of 8.37, and the customs-office 8.1bn is the figure relied upon in the analysis.

Scenario probabilities, tail-risk probabilities and invalidator probabilities are analyst judgements calibrated to the factor analysis and are not derived from options-implied distributions, which were unavailable.

This dossier was passed through an adversarial verification gate before publication. Twenty-six headline figures were re-checked against primary sources and confirmed; four substantive corrections were applied (the superseded 15% headline US tariff, euro-area core HICP of 2.5% rather than 2.4%, the Brent-versus-ECB-hike chronology, and the CFTC release-versus-observation date convention); and a further set of citation-integrity and staleness issues were flagged inline rather than silently carried. Factor confidences were LOWERED for Policy & Rates (strategic), Inflation & Growth (strategic), Risk Appetite (tactical), Flows & Positioning (both), External Balance (both), Event Risk (both), Fiscal & Sovereign (both) and USD Liquidity (tactical) as a direct consequence. Every figure that verification could not confirm is marked 'flagged' or 'best available' at its point of use rather than presented as solid.
